meta.blurb: In 1910 a writer claimed that getting rich follows laws, like arithmetic. Some of Wallace Wattles's advice is sensible, and some is pure belief. This retelling keeps his boldest ideas and tells you honestly which is which.
meta.bible: Wallace D. Wattles: an American writer; the book was first published in 1910. The book has a short preface and 17 chapters. Thinking Substance: Wattles's name for the one living material that he believed fills the universe and makes all things; this is his belief and is not proven science. Gratitude: thankfulness, which Wattles says keeps the mind close to what is good. Increase: his word for growth in life and wealth. Use Value and Cash Value: his terms for what a thing is worth in use and what it costs in money. The Certain Way: his phrase for his method. Voice and tone: warm, clear, honest and encouraging; Wattles's claims are always given as his own beliefs, never as proven facts; modern cautions are noted gently; no invented quotes, numbers or studies.

A1A2: In 1910 a man named Wallace Wattles wrote a book about getting rich.
He said his ideas came from wise people and from his own life.
He said it is good to want money, because money helps you live well.
He said being poor is not good, and being poor helps no one.
He said wanting more is natural, so you should not feel bad.
He hoped that rich people would use their money to help others.
He said getting rich is like arithmetic, with rules that never change.
Two men live in one town, but one is rich and one is poor.
Many people work very hard, but they stay poor all their lives.
Two shops sell the same goods, but only one shop does well.
He said no one is shut out of the chance to get rich.
He said the earth has more than enough for everyone.
He believed that everything in the world comes from one great mind.
He said a clear thought can bring a real thing into the world.
He said all living things want to grow and have more life.
He said the world wants you to have everything you can use.
Wattles said these ideas are the base of everything else.
He said you should make new things and not take from others.
He said you should give people more than they pay for.
He said you must never cheat anyone if you want to be rich.
He said to say thank you often for all the good things you have.
A thankful person sees what they have, not what is missing.
Make a clear picture in your mind of what you want.
He said to look at your picture in your mind every day.
He said to believe that what you want will come to you.
He said not to talk about your plans with people who doubt you.
He said to use your will on yourself, not on other people.
He said not to think about being poor, but about being rich.
He said to stay away from sad talk and to look for good news.
He said to keep your mind on your goal and not on fear.
He said thinking is not enough, and you must also act.
He said to start now, where you are, with what you have.
He said to do all you can each day, and do it well.
He said every job, big or small, should be done well.
He said not to hurry or worry, but to keep a calm mind.
Small good acts every day will build a big result.
He said to choose work that fits your best skills.
He said your job now can be a step to a better job.
He said each customer should feel they got more than they paid.
He said to be kind and hopeful when you meet other people.
He said the method works for all kinds of jobs.
A worker who wants to rise should do more than the job asks.
He said not to wait for luck, but to keep working toward your goal.
He said you may meet doubt on the road, but you should go on.
Real life is harder than the book says, and luck matters too.
At the end, the book gives a short list of the main steps.
First make a clear picture and give thanks every day.
Then act today, do each job well, and be fair to others.
Some of his advice is good: have goals, work hard, and be fair.
Wattles's book is more than one hundred years old, and people still read it.
B1B2: In 1910 an American writer named Wallace Wattles published a short book with a bold promise. He said that any person could learn a certain way to become rich.
Wattles said that he had learned from the great thinkers of the past. He also said that he had tried the ideas himself and seen them work.
The first chapter argues that wanting to be rich is natural and right. Money, says Wattles, buys the things that let a person grow in body, mind and spirit.
Wattles does not believe that being poor is a noble or a good thing. A person who has nothing, he says, finds it hard to help others or to enjoy a full life.
He says that the wish for more comes from life itself, which always wants to grow. For this reason, he tells his readers, they should never feel ashamed of it.
Wattles hopes that a rich person will also be a generous one. He believes that a world with more rich people would be a better world for everyone.
In the second chapter Wattles claims that there is a science of getting rich. Like arithmetic, he says, it follows laws, so the same actions always give the same results.
Wattles points out that people in the same town can end up very different. If the place decided everything, he says, then everyone in a rich place would be rich.
Wattles notes that many of the hardest workers in the world are poor. Hard work alone, he says, does not make a person rich, because the way a person works matters too.
In the same trade, says Wattles, one person succeeds and another fails. The difference is not the business itself but the way each person does the work.
The third chapter asks whether the rich have taken all the chances. Wattles says they have not, and he adds that if one field is closed, a person can enter another.
Wattles believes that the world holds more than enough for every person who lives in it. Many modern readers would add that some resources are limited, so we should read this claim with care.

In the fourth chapter Wattles states his first principle, which is a belief rather than a proven fact. He says that one thinking substance fills the whole universe, and that everything we see is made from it.
According to Wattles, this substance responds to human thought. A thing that is held clearly in the mind, he says, can be made to appear in the world.
The fifth chapter says that every living thing wants to grow, from the smallest seed to the cleverest person. Wattles believes that life itself is always pushing toward more.
Wattles teaches that the power behind all things wants every person to have a full life. If this is true, he says, then wanting wealth cannot be wrong.
Wattles says that these ideas are the base of everything that follows. First comes the thinking substance, then the push to grow, and last the plenty that is waiting for everyone.
In the sixth chapter Wattles warns against fighting other people for a share of the same wealth. Instead, he says, a person should create something new and offer it to the world.
Wattles says that every business deal should leave both people better off. The seller should give more in use value than the buyer pays in money.
Wattles teaches that cheating has no place in his method. A person who lies or takes unfairly, he says, is working against the very law he wants to use.

The seventh chapter is about gratitude, which means feeling thankful for what you have. Wattles says that a thankful mind stays close to the source of good things, and that this nearness is part of the method.
A person without gratitude, says Wattles, keeps thinking about what is missing. Such thoughts, he believes, fix the mind on poverty and push good things away.
The eighth chapter gives the first step of the method, which Wattles calls thinking in the certain way. A person must form a clear picture in the mind of exactly what he or she wants.
Wattles tells the reader to think of the picture often and to keep it exact. He says that a person who sees clearly what he wants is more likely to go and get it.
Wattles asks his readers to have faith, which means to believe the thing is already on its way. Doubt, he says, ruins the picture and weakens the whole effort.
Wattles advises readers to keep their plans to themselves unless a listener believes in them. A doubtful friend, he says, can easily take away a person's courage.
In the ninth chapter Wattles explains that the will should be used only on oneself. A person should think and act in the right way and should never try to force others.
Wattles tells his readers not to spend their time studying poverty. To help the poor, he says, a person must think about wealth, because thoughts about poverty only make more of it.
Wattles tells the reader to avoid gloomy books, news and talk that fill the mind with doubt. He says it is better to choose hopeful ideas and to speak about them.
In the tenth chapter Wattles returns to the will and asks the reader to hold a firm purpose. He says that faith and a steady aim should never give way to fear.
Chapter eleven makes an important point: thinking alone is not enough. Wattles says that a person must also act, and that thought exists to guide what we do.
Wattles tells his readers to begin where they are and with what they have. They must not wait for a better time or place, because the right moment is now.
In the twelfth chapter Wattles asks for efficient action. A person should do everything possible each day and do each task as well as it can be done.
Wattles says that each small act should be a success in itself. A person who does little things well, he says, is building the path to bigger things.
Wattles warns his readers not to be in a hurry or to worry about the future. A calm and steady mind, he says, works better than an anxious one.
Wattles says that success comes from repeating the same good habits every day. Small actions, done well and often, add up to large results over time.
The thirteenth chapter is about choosing the right business. Wattles says that a strong wish to do something shows that you have the power to do it.
Wattles says that a person who is in the wrong work should not despair. The present job can still be a step toward the right one, if it is done well.
The fourteenth chapter says that every person who deals with you should feel a sense of increase. Wattles wants customers to feel that they have gained something real.
Wattles suggests that the feeling of increase comes from the person who gives it. If you are hopeful and sure of your purpose, other people will feel that they gain by meeting you.
Wattles says that the method is not only for business people. Doctors, teachers, ministers and many others, he says, can use it to give people a sense of increase.

In the fifteenth chapter Wattles speaks to employees who want to move up, whom he calls the advancing man. He tells them to do a little more each day than the job requires and to prepare for the next position.
The advancing man, says Wattles, does not wait for luck or for someone else to lift him. He keeps his picture in mind, works hard, and moves up one step at a time.
The sixteenth chapter gives some cautions to readers who are following the method. Wattles says that readers will meet doubts and failures, and that they must not give up.
Real life is more complicated than the book suggests. Health, luck, other people and the state of the world all play a part, and no method can promise a result.
The last chapter is a summary of the science of getting rich. Wattles puts the whole method into a short list of steps that the reader can follow.

The summary begins with the belief in one thinking substance and the clear picture of what you want. It adds that the reader should give thanks often, since gratitude keeps the mind close to what is good.
The remaining steps of the summary are very practical and easy to understand. The reader must act today, do every task well, and give each person more in use than he takes in money.
Whatever one thinks of his large claims, much of the advice is sensible. Clear goals, thankfulness, steady work and fair dealing are good habits for anyone to have.
More than a hundred years later, The Science of Getting Rich is still read around the world. Take what is useful, test it in your own life, and decide for yourself what is true.
C1C2: In 1910 an American writer named Wallace Wattles published a short and confident book with a title that sounded almost like a laboratory report. Its promise was simple and bold: that any person who followed a certain method could become rich, whatever his or her starting point. We will read it as Wattles wrote it, as a set of beliefs and advice that readers have argued over for more than a hundred years.

In his short preface, Wattles explained that his teaching rested on the work of older philosophers, whose long arguments he had boiled down into plain advice. He added that he had tested the method in his own life and found that it worked. Readers today should remember that this is his own claim, since nothing in the book can be checked like a result in a laboratory.

The first chapter opens with a defence of ambition, for Wattles insists that the desire to be rich is neither shameful nor selfish. A person with little money, he argues, cannot fully develop the body, the mind or the spirit, because each of them needs tools, books, food and leisure. To want a richer life, he concludes, is simply to want to be fully alive.

Wattles rejects the old idea that poverty is a mark of virtue, and he calls the wish to be poor a kind of mistake. A man without means, he says, can neither enjoy the good things of the world nor do much good for the people around him. In his view, the world grows richer when each person in it grows richer.

Every living thing, Wattles observes, strives to grow and to live more fully, and the human wish for more is only that same urge at work. He therefore tells his readers to stop apologising for their desires and to treat them as a natural force. Money alone is not the goal, he adds, for money is only a means to a fuller life.

Although the book is eager about wealth, Wattles keeps repeating that the aim is a larger life for everyone and not a pile of coins for one person. He hopes that the people who follow his method will use their money to build, to teach and to give. Whether every reader who succeeded would really do so is, of course, another question altogether.

The second chapter makes the book's boldest claim, that getting rich is a science with fixed laws, just as arithmetic has fixed rules. If that is true, Wattles reasons, then anyone who does the same things in the same way must reach the same result. Readers should note that he offers this as a matter of faith and experience, and not as proof from a laboratory.

Wattles observes that two neighbours in the same town, breathing the same air and facing the same chances, may end up in very different places. If the place decided everything, he argues, then everyone in a wealthy city would be wealthy. The cause must therefore lie in the way people think and act, and not in where they happen to live.

It is a familiar sight, Wattles points out, that some of the hardest labourers live and die in poverty, while others who work much less become wealthy. Effort by itself, he concludes, cannot be the secret, for it is the manner of the effort that makes the difference. This is the central idea that the rest of the book sets out to explain.

Wattles then turns to trade, noting that two people in the very same business, with the same goods and the same customers, can have opposite fates. One of them prospers and grows rich, he says, while the other barely manages to survive from one year to the next. The explanation, he insists, lies in a certain way of doing things, and that way can be learned by anyone.

In the third chapter Wattles asks whether the wealthy have already seized every opportunity, leaving nothing for the rest. He answers that this is false, because a worker shut out of one trade can always find another trade open to him. When old industries close, he says, new ones open, and the doors never stay shut for long.

To Wattles, the supply of the earth is so large that it could never be exhausted by those who use it, and he points to forests, fields, mines and seas as proof. Nobody is poor, he says, because the world has run out of good things. Today's readers may reasonably question this, since many resources are limited and the world is far more crowded than it was in his time.

The fourth chapter sets out what Wattles calls his first principle, and it is a belief of faith rather than a finding of science. He teaches that there is one thinking substance, from which all things are made, and that it fills the spaces between the stars as well as the stuff of the earth. Everything that exists, in his view, is a shape taken by this single living material.

Wattles goes on to claim that this thinking substance responds to human thought, so that a thought clearly held in the mind can bring about the thing that is imagined. It is the idea on which his whole method rests, and he states it with perfect confidence. A cautious reader will note that he offers no scientific evidence for it, and will decide how far to trust it.

In the fifth chapter Wattles turns to the idea of increase, arguing that all life is moved by a steady push toward a fuller and richer existence. The seed that breaks open and the person who studies late into the night are, in his view, driven by the same urge. This push, he says, is the reason we feel unsatisfied when we have too little.

Wattles takes the argument a step further and says that the power behind all things wishes every person to have as much as he or she can use. A wealthy life is therefore not a favour wrung from a reluctant world but a gift that is already intended. For anyone who has felt guilty about wanting more, he offers a kind of permission.

With these three ideas in place, the thinking substance, the urge to grow and the plenty that surrounds us, Wattles considers his foundation laid. Everything that follows in the book is a set of instructions for living in harmony with them. He asks the reader not to argue yet, but to read on and see what the method requires.

The sixth chapter draws a sharp line between the person who competes for what already exists and the one who creates something new. Wattles believes that the competitor is always in danger of losing, since there is a fixed prize and many hands reaching for it. The creator, by contrast, adds to the world's wealth and so has no need to take anything from anyone.

Wattles insists that every transaction should leave both parties better off, and that a person should always give more in use value than he receives in cash value. A fair seller, he says, can look at every customer and know that the customer has gained from the trade. This habit, he claims, keeps a person in harmony with the source of all riches.

There is no room in the method, Wattles declares, for cheating, trickery or the sharp bargain that leaves one person poorer so that another may be richer. A person who takes advantage of others has stepped outside the law that makes wealth possible. Honest dealing is therefore not only a duty but the very condition of success.

In the seventh chapter Wattles turns from action to feeling and recommends deep and constant gratitude for everything that has come to the reader. Gratitude, he says, keeps the mind turned toward the source of all good things and prevents it from drifting into envy. Many readers who do not share his philosophy still find this advice worth keeping.

The ungrateful mind, Wattles warns, dwells on what is lacking, and a mind fixed on lack soon begins to see only poverty and to attract it. By contrast, a mind that rests on what is good and rich in its life moves toward more of the same. He therefore asks the reader to set aside a little time every day simply for giving thanks.

The eighth chapter introduces what Wattles regards as the heart of the method, and he calls it thinking in a certain way. The reader must form a clear and detailed picture of the thing he wants, and he must be able to see it as plainly as if it already stood before him. A vague wish, in this teaching, is almost no wish at all, and it will produce almost nothing.

Like a builder who studies the plans of a house before laying the first stone, the reader should return to the picture many times a day and fill in every detail. Wattles compares the practice to making the thing real in the mind before it is real in the world. Many modern readers would simply call it focus, and it is close to the advice of goal setting today.

Along with the picture, Wattles demands faith: the reader must believe that what he wants is already his, as surely as a traveller believes that the road ahead leads to the town. Doubt, he warns, breaks the connection and spoils the power of the picture, so it must be driven out. This is the point where the method moves from practical advice to a leap of belief.

Since the faith of the beginner is fragile, Wattles advises that plans should not be shared with people who are likely to laugh or to doubt. A careless remark from a sceptical friend can shake a resolve that has been built with great care. Only those who sympathise with the goal, he suggests, are safe company for the dreamer.

The ninth chapter concerns the will, and Wattles gives a firm rule that it must be applied to the self alone. The reader may direct his own thoughts and his own actions as much as he likes, but he must never use his will to press other people or to bend the world to his wishes. Such pressure, he says, is wrong in itself and is useless as a way to wealth.

On this point Wattles is blunt: the student of poverty becomes poor in mind, and a person cannot cure a problem by staring at it forever. Whoever wants to remove poverty, he says, will do it by becoming rich and then using riches wisely. Most modern readers will find this too simple, since understanding a problem is often the first step toward solving it.

He also tells the reader to turn away from gloomy books, dark prophecies and anyone who dwells on failure, since these things feed doubt in the mind. In their place, he suggests, one should seek hopeful ideas and speak of them often. A reader may feel that some honesty about bad news is also healthy, but his advice is clear.

The tenth chapter returns to the will and adds that purpose and faith must be held without wavering, day after day, however slow the results may seem. Wattles asks the reader to think not about what is wrong around him, but about what he intends to bring into being. The mind, he believes, slowly becomes whatever it is allowed to dwell on, so it should be guarded with care.

In the eleventh chapter Wattles corrects any reader who believes that dreaming will be enough, and he declares that thought must always be followed by action. A person who sits and pictures wealth without working for it, he says, will stay exactly where he is. The picture is meant to guide the working hand and to give its labour a direction, never to take its place.

The right time to begin, says Wattles, is today, and the right place is the one in which the reader finds himself at this moment. It is useless to dream of a better position elsewhere while the present work is left undone. The person who does well where he stands, he argues, will find that the next step opens in front of him.

The twelfth chapter is a call for efficient action, and its instructions are as practical as any in the book. Each day the reader should do everything that can be done that day, and he should do it in the most successful manner he can manage. Wattles does not ask for hurry or for exhausting effort, only for thoroughness and a steady attention to the work.

Every single act, even the smallest, should be treated as a success in itself, says Wattles, since a whole life of success is made up of such acts. A job done carelessly leaves a gap in the structure, while a job done thoroughly adds one more sound stone to it. The reader who grasps this idea will no longer look down on ordinary tasks, however small they may seem.

Hurry and worry, in Wattles's view, are the enemies of efficient action, because both make a person careless and unsure of his purpose. He recommends a calm and steady pace, with the picture kept firmly in mind and the day's work done in good order. Many people today would agree that a quiet mind often does the best work.

Day after day, the reader is to repeat the same simple habits: hold the picture, give thanks and do the day's work as well as possible. Wattles expects that the results will accumulate gradually, as water collects drop by drop, until the goal comes within reach. It is a modest and practical thought, and it is perhaps the most reliable part of his teaching.

In the thirteenth chapter Wattles turns to the choice of work, and he advises the reader to find an occupation that makes use of his strongest talents. A strong and lasting desire to do something, he suggests, is itself a sign that the ability is present. Not everyone will agree that wishing is proof of skill, but the advice to choose work that suits you is sound.

If the reader is currently in the wrong occupation, Wattles tells him not to be afraid, for the work he now does can serve as a stepping stone. He should not leave it carelessly, but only when he sees an opening that fits his picture. Meanwhile, the present task, if it is done well and with a cheerful spirit, is itself a valuable part of the preparation.

The fourteenth chapter is concerned with what Wattles calls the impression of increase, and it asks the reader to ensure that everyone who deals with him feels that his life has been enlarged. A good business, he argues, sends its customers away feeling that they have gained, and they naturally return. In a modern sense, this is simply the old idea of good service, which no business can do without for long.

Wattles goes further and says that people feel the increase not only in the goods that they buy but in the very person who sells them. A man who carries faith, hope and a clear sense of purpose into every conversation gives a kind of lift to all who meet him. Customers, he implies, are drawn to such a person as travellers are drawn to a lamp.

Wattles takes care to add that his method is not reserved for merchants and manufacturers, but is open to teachers, doctors, ministers and every kind of professional person. Each of them, he says, can spread a sense of growth among the people they serve, and so grow richer themselves. In his view, the principle is as wide as human work itself, and nobody who serves others is left out of it.

The fifteenth chapter is addressed to the employee who wishes to rise, and its advice is to do each day a little more than the job strictly requires. The worker should act as though he already held the higher post, filling his mind with its duties and his hands with its tasks. Employers, Wattles suggests, will sooner or later notice a person who lives in this way, and they will want to reward him.

Such an advancing man, according to Wattles, neither waits for luck nor complains that the world has failed to notice him. He keeps the picture of his goal before him, does his daily work with energy, and rises step by step until he stands where he wanted to be. The path is long, but the book insists that it is open to anyone who will walk it.

The sixteenth chapter offers a series of cautions, and the chief of these is not to be discouraged when results are slow to arrive. Wattles believes that anyone who follows the method will succeed, and he suggests that failure means the method has not been followed fully. This is a hard saying, and it overlooks the many reasons, beyond a person's control, why plans may fail.

It is only fair to add that real life is more tangled than the book allows, since health, luck, family duties and the state of the world all help to decide how a person fares. No honest teacher can promise that one method will work for everyone, and Wattles was no exception. The wise reader will therefore take the useful advice and treat the large promises with care.

The last chapter gathers the whole teaching into a compact summary, so that the reader can see at a glance what he is being asked to do. Wattles lists the steps one after another, from the first belief in a thinking substance to the final habit of daily work. It reads almost like a recipe for a lifetime, with the same ingredients to be used again each morning.

According to the summary, the reader begins by believing in the thinking substance and by forming a clear picture of what he desires, which he must hold in mind with unshaken faith. He then adds a daily habit of thanks, offered in honest feeling for everything that has already come to him. These first steps, Wattles says, prepare the mind for all that follows, and they must never be skipped.

The remaining steps of the summary concern everyday conduct, and they are the plainest in the whole book. The reader must act today, do each piece of work as well as it can be done, and give every person more in use than he takes in cash. Whether or not one agrees with his explanation, these are habits that few would regret, and Wattles promises that they will carry a person from wishing to having.

Whatever one thinks of the thinking substance and the promises that surround it, much of Wattles's practical advice is sensible and kind. Clear goals, thankfulness, steady daily effort and honest dealing are habits that have helped people long before and long after his time. They are worth keeping even for those who read the book as philosophy rather than science.

More than a century after it appeared, The Science of Getting Rich is still read by people who hope for a better life and who like a book that speaks plainly. It is best taken as a philosophy of effort and attitude, a mixture of useful habits and large beliefs that cannot be proved. Read it with an open mind, test its ideas against your own experience, and keep what proves true.
